title: Soy protein vs. pea protein: which is better?

seo.title: Soy protein vs. pea protein: amino acids, quality, and digestion
seo.meta_description: Soy and pea isolates can provide 75–90 g protein per 100 g. Compare amino acids, digestibility, allergens, and practical differences.
seo.search_intent: Compare soy and pea protein powders without assuming all brands have the same protein content or that plant proteins are automatically low quality.

excerpt: Soy and pea isolates can provide similar grams of protein per scoop. Soy tends to have a somewhat stronger indispensable amino-acid profile, while modern pea isolates can still be highly digestible and high quality.
content_html:
If one tub of soy protein and one tub of pea protein both say “24 g protein,” the comparison is not finished. Protein per scoop matters, but so do amino-acid profile, digestibility, serving size, sodium, flavorings, and how the product fits the rest of the diet.

Protein concentration can be nearly identical

Commercial isolates commonly land around 75–90 g protein per 100 g, although the exact label should always take priority. A 30 g scoop may therefore provide about 22–27 g protein from either source.

A one- or two-gram difference per scoop is modest compared with larger differences in price, taste, added ingredients, or the amount of powder someone actually uses.

Soy usually has a stronger amino-acid profile

Soy supplies all indispensable amino acids in proportions that can produce high protein-quality scores. Reviews show that processing and the food matrix shift DIAAS values considerably, so “soy protein” does not have one universal score.

Pea protein is rich in lysine, while sulfur-containing amino acids such as methionine and cysteine often set its limiting amino-acid score. Soy products generally score strongly because their indispensable amino-acid pattern is well distributed.

Pea protein can still be highly digestible

A controlled human study of pea protein isolate reported mean real ileal amino-acid digestibility of 93.6%, compared with 96.8% for casein, with no significant difference in overall amino-acid digestibility. Its calculated DIAAS was 1.00.

That is a useful correction to the blanket claim that plant protein is poorly absorbed. Protein source, processing, and food matrix all matter.

What about leucine?

Values vary by product, but soy isolates often contain around 8 g leucine per 100 g protein while many pea isolates fall roughly in the 6–8 g range. A serving containing 25 g total protein might therefore provide around 1.5–2 g leucine from pea and close to 2 g from soy.

If leucine matters for a specific training or clinical goal, use the brand’s amino-acid profile when available rather than assuming a fixed number from the plant name alone.

Blends can complement amino-acid patterns

Pea is often combined with rice protein because the two amino-acid patterns complement one another: pea contributes lysine while rice contributes a different sulfur-amino-acid balance. The final score depends on the blend ratio and processing.

Allergy and tolerance can decide the choice

Soy is a major food allergen in the United States and must be declared accordingly. Pea can also cause allergy and cross-reactivity exists among legumes, but it is not regulated in exactly the same way as soy.

Protein isolates may provide 20–25 g protein with little fiber, while a cup of whole cooked peas or soy foods can provide several grams of fiber along with protein. A shake therefore does not reproduce the whole legume.

The useful takeaway

If two products each provide 24–25 g protein per serving, the quantity is nearly tied; soy typically has a robust amino-acid profile, while human data put one pea isolate at 93.6% mean ileal amino-acid digestibility and DIAAS 1.00. The label, amino-acid data, allergy status, tolerance, and overall diet complete the choice.

faq.question: Is soy protein better than pea protein?
faq.answer: Both can be high-quality choices. Soy usually has a somewhat stronger amino-acid profile, while well-processed pea isolate can still have high digestibility.

faq.question: Is pea protein incomplete?
faq.answer: It contains all indispensable amino acids but is relatively lower in methionine and cysteine.

faq.question: Is pea protein poorly absorbed?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. A human trial found mean ileal amino-acid digestibility of 93.6% for pea protein isolate.
